## Motion is designed over time

Animation is a sequence of deliberate changes shown for deliberate lengths of time. A **frame** is one image in the sequence; a **keyframe** records an important pose or change; the **timeline** controls order and duration; **onion skinning** shows nearby frames faintly so motion can be judged.

## Beginner tool: Pencil2D

[Pencil2D](https://www.pencil2d.org/) is a focused open-source tool for hand-drawn raster and vector animation. Keep the first task small enough to revise:

1. storyboard a start, change and return;
2. create the main keyframes first;
3. turn on onion skinning and add only the in-between frames needed;
4. preview the loop at different timings;
5. hold important poses longer instead of redrawing them repeatedly;
6. export using the teacher-approved format and reopen the export.

## Classroom task: identity in motion

Animate the student's original logo, lettermark or one simple object for **2–4 seconds**. The loop should communicate one idea through timing and shape change: assemble, reveal, bounce, rotate, transform or respond. Avoid tracing a commercial mark or downloading a finished character as the answer.

## Evaluate the loop

Ask another viewer what they notice first and whether the loop feels intentional. Check the silhouette, timing, distracting jumps, first/last-frame transition, crop, background and export quality. Save the editable Pencil2D file as well as the exported animation.

Use [Blender](06-blender-artistic-3d.qmd) when the goal becomes artistic 3D animation or rendering. Use [parametric CAD](../04-3d-printing/01-additive-cad.qmd) when the goal is a dimension-driven fabrication part.
